Gemini CLI: request flow and controls

The step-by-step guide explains each step in general; how to read these trees.

What happens to a request

The steps run in the typical order. A documented order, where the vendor states one, is shown on its step. A decision point appears where the documentation describes a real branch; an agent with none has none documented.

A. Setup, before the first model call

The harness gets ready: it finds your rules, your tools and your permissions. No model is involved yet.

  1. Choose the front door ● documented !

    You can run it in a terminal, either interactively or headless for scripts. It also documents an IDE connection, an early SDK, and a command that sets up automation to triage issues and review proposed changes.

  2. Apply organization rules ◔ partly documented !

    A system settings file sets a baseline and takes precedence over other settings, and admin policies override user, workspace and default ones. Enterprise controls are managed through a console. The documentation does not mention lists of allowed or blocked models.

    Documented order: Admin policies win over user, workspace and default policies.

  3. Load the house rules ● documented !

    It reads instruction files from your home folder and project, searching from the current folder upward and joining what it finds. Files can import other files, and a file in a subfolder holds rules for that folder. It also scans a folder when a tool touches it.

    Documented order: The search starts in the current folder and moves up through the parent folders to a stop point.

  4. Load memory and earlier sessions ◐ documented, with limits !

    It keeps durable notes, and an experimental feature drafts new ones from past sessions for you to approve. You can resume, branch and list earlier sessions, saved as local transcripts. For handoff, the documentation describes exporting sessions to files.

    Decision point: Does a memory reload also look in extra directories?

    • The include-directories memory setting is true: A reload scans the include directories as well.

      scans include directories when

    • That setting is false: Just the current directory is used.

      when false, only the current directory is used

    Documented in F02.memory-scope-loading. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Stock the built-in tools ● documented !

    It gives the model tools to search and read files, edit them, run shell commands, which need manual confirmation, and search or fetch from the web. A setting can restrict the set of built-in tools, and a command lists the ones available.

  6. Load skills and custom commands ◔ partly documented !

    A skill is a folder with a description file that the model loads when a task fits. Custom commands are small text files you type yourself, with room for arguments. The documentation does not mention per-skill tool or model overrides, or how commands relate to skills.

    Documented order: User and project commands take precedence over extension commands, which rank lowest.

  7. Connect outside tools ◐ documented, with limits !

    It works with MCP servers, which can run as local programs or be reached remotely, and are set up in settings files with optional sign-in. Servers an admin requires are limited to remote connections. Tools can be filtered per server, and admins can list allowed servers.

    Decision point: Which connection types can an MCP server use?

    • A server in general: Local programs, event streams and streamable web connections are each described.

      communicates via stdin/stdout

    • A server an admin requires: It is limited to remote connections made over the network.

      Required servers only support remote transports

    Documented in F12.transports. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  8. Set the safety posture ◐ documented, with limits !

    It has four approval modes: ask each time, auto-approve edits, plan (read-only) and run freely. New folders get a trust check. The documentation disagrees on whether run-freely can be turned on by a keyboard shortcut, and on whether settings merge from two files or four.

    Documented order: When several policy rules match a tool call, the highest-priority one is applied.

  9. Pick the model and thinking effort ◔ partly documented

    You pick the model in a dialog or at launch, and the default is automatic. A Gemini API key is an alternative to a Google sign-in, but an unpaid key is capped at 250 requests a day on the Flash model. The documentation does not mention effort levels or shared model choice.

    Decision point: Which model does the automatic choice pick?

    • Preview features are enabled: It resolves to the preview model.

      resolves to the preview model if preview features are enabled

    • Preview features are not enabled: It resolves to the standard pro model.

      otherwise to the standard pro model

    Documented in F17.model-catalog. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  10. Prepare an isolated workspace ◐ documented, with limits

    It can create an isolated worktree for a run, with a generated name if you give none, but this is documented as needing an experimental setting to be turned on.

B. Each turn, before sending

For every request the harness decides what the model will read, and runs any code you asked it to run first.

  1. Assemble the prompt ◔ partly documented

    You can pull in file contents with an at-sign reference, add extra directories to the workspace, and exclude files through ignore rules. The documentation does not mention the size of the context window.

  2. Run your own code at set moments ◐ documented, with limits !

    Hooks run your own scripts at set moments, such as before a model request. For now just command-type hooks are supported, non-text message parts are filtered out, and one event does not support some blocking controls. Project hooks start untrusted.

C. The model call

The harness sends the request and waits. This is the only step where the model itself does any work.

  1. Send the request and handle trouble ● documented

    It routes between models automatically and switches to a fallback model on failure. When the default pro model is rate-limited it switches to flash for the session. The daily limit listed for Google sign-in is 1000 requests.

  2. Set the thinking budget ◐ documented, with limits

    A model setting block can carry reasoning configuration, and the thinking budget can be controlled directly. The entry describes it just as configuration for models with reasoning, without a per-model list of accepted levels.

  3. Reuse the unchanged part of the prompt · not researched not yet researched

D. After the model answers, every turn

The model's answer is only a request. The harness checks it, runs it if allowed, and feeds the result back.

  1. Read what the model asked for · not researched not yet researched
  2. Decide whether it is allowed ◐ documented, with limits !

    Rules can be set per tool, per path and per shell command, and an older option for pre-allowing tools is deprecated in favour of the policy engine. An LLM-based security checker is off by default and described as an additional layer of protection.

  3. Save an undo point ● documented

    It can save snapshots automatically for recovery, and you can go back to an earlier state of the conversation. Named checkpoints can be listed, saved, resumed, deleted and shared.

  4. Run it inside the fence ● documented !

    A sandbox can be switched on and is documented as off by default. On Mac, a profile confines writes to the project folder. The sandbox page describes network as allowed, while a network access setting is documented with a default of off, so the two differ.

    Decision point: What if a sandboxed command needs more permission?

    • The command fails on a permission restriction: A dialog explains which extra permissions are needed and asks for them.

      When a sandboxed command fails due to permission restrictions, a Request step shows a modal dialog

    • You add the directories at session start: Extra directories can be added when the session starts instead.

      can be used when starting the session instead

    Documented in F05.sandbox-override. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  5. Tidy the tool's output · not researched not yet researched
  6. Feed the result back and go round again ● documented !

    The core returns tool results to the model for further processing. Turn limits cap a session, a helper's turns, and tool calls per task. Detection of infinite loops can be turned off, and a particular output value can stop the loop at once.

  7. Hand work to helpers ◔ partly documented !

    Helpers are defined in text files and can have their own tools and model. The documentation says they cannot call other helpers. It does not mention how many can run at once, in total, or in parallel; separate sessions can use worktrees to avoid collisions.

  8. Shrink the context when it fills ● documented !

    The core compresses the conversation automatically before sending it to the model, at a usage level you can set. You can also compress by hand, which swaps the whole chat for a summary. A hook fires before the automatic summary.

  9. Show the answer or ask you ● documented !

    Plan mode is a read-only space for designing before implementation, and executing a plan switches to active execution. The footer shows the model name, context usage and the number of loaded instruction files.

  10. Wrap up and keep score ◐ documented, with limits !

    It shows token usage on request and at exit, and records traces through telemetry. A spending setting is scoped to quota exhaustion when AI credits are available: it can prompt each time, use credits automatically, or disable credit usage.

    Decision point: What happens when quota runs out and AI credits are available?

    • Set to ask (the default): It prompts you each time.

      'ask' prompts each time

    • Set to use credits automatically: Credits are used without asking.

      automatically uses credits

    • Set to turn credit use off: Credits are not used.

      disables credit usage

    Documented in F22.budget-caps. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

E. Around the session

Things that sit outside a single turn: unattended runs, add-ons, updates and who runs the service.

  1. Run without you watching ◔ partly documented !

    Shell commands can be moved to the background. Changelog entries mention remote workers and delegating work to remote helpers. The documentation does not mention scheduled routines, remote sessions or event triggers.

  2. Extend and share ◐ documented, with limits !

    Extensions bundle prompts, tool connections, custom commands, themes and helpers, and install from a repository address or local path. Management commands take effect after a restart. The gallery route covers public extensions, which it indexes automatically.

    Documented order: The allowed-extensions list overrides the setting that blocks extensions from Git.

    Decision point: What decides whether an extension may be installed?

    • The allowed-extensions list has entries: Extensions must match a pattern in the list to be allowed.

      if nonempty, only matching extensions are allowed

    • Install with the consent option: The confirmation prompt is skipped after acknowledging risks.

      acknowledges security risks and skips the confirmation prompt

    • The admin setting is false: Extensions are not allowed to be installed.

      when false, disallows extensions from being installed

    Documented in F11.trust-signing. Each branch quotes the cell; the order between decision points is not stated.

  3. Updates and releases ● documented !

    It ships on nightly, preview and stable channels, with a weekly cadence promoting code along that path. Release notes are published as a changelog, and deprecations are announced there and in notes inside the docs.

  4. Where it runs and who runs it ◔ partly documented

    It runs on Mac, Windows and Ubuntu with a recent Node runtime. Google AI Pro or Ultra gives higher limits shared with agent mode in the IDE, while Workspace plans do not cover its API usage. The documentation does not mention shared servers or a shared runtime.

  5. Identity, retention and audit ● documented !

    Sign-in is with a Google account for Gemini Code Assist, and Workspace accounts get organization tiers. Old session data is cleaned up automatically by default. A telemetry and auditing section covers configuring the CLI for monitoring.
